# Question 2. Data audit, cleaning, and analytic cohort

## 2a. Standardization

```{r}
# Import raw CSV file from data folder
# Use here::here to manage file paths
raw_data <- read_csv(
  here::here("data", "PUBH551_Group_Project_Depression_Data_2005_2025.csv"), 
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) 
  # Added col_types = col(.default) per step 2b instruction
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Identify the 5-missing value representations in raw data by quickly looking at every 
# unique response
raw_data %>% 
  # Select the text columns
  select(where(is.character)) %>%
  # Do not include the variables containing "id", "date", and "USD" as those will have an 
  # abundance of unique values and will be hard to sift through
  select(-matches("_id"), -matches("date"), -matches("usd")) %>%
  # Use map() to return a list of each unique response from every variable
  map(~ unique(.x))
# 5 missing value representations = "", ".", "NA", "N/A" , and "missing"
```

We need to replace the missing value representations with standard NA values to prevent errors in future analysis.

```{r}
# Replace the missing value representations with standard NA values across all columns
# Use mutate(across(where(is.character))) to modify all columns stored as text/characters
# ifelse(.x %in% ) to check each value in the column and identify whether the current value 
# (.x) matches any of the 5 specific missing value strings identified in audit and replace 
# with standard NA value
na_data <- raw_data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ ifelse(.x %in% c("", ".", "NA", "N/A", "missing"), NA, .x)))

# Standardize the dataset to fix inconsistent capitalization, whitespace, underscores, and missing-value representations
data <- na_data %>%
  # Use mutate() to modify column inside the dataset
  mutate(across(
    # Exclude the often case-sensitive ID codes from cleaning using !c()
    where(is.character) & !c(record_id, participant_id),
    # Apply changes to every item in list
    ~ .x %>%
      # str_to_lower() converts every letter to lowercase
      str_to_lower() %>%
      # str_squish() removes leading/trailing spaces
      str_squish() %>%
      # str_replace_all() to replace all underscores with normal spaces
      str_replace_all("_", " ")
  ))
```

Looking through the unique values, we can document a variety of inconsistencies across the "comorbid_condition" column prior to filtering.

**Capitalization:** There was a mixed use of title case, uppercase, and lowercase

- e.g. "ASTHMA", "Asthma", and "asthma"
- e.g. "OBESITY", "Obesity", and "obesity"
- e.g. "HYPERTENSION", "Hypertension", and "hypertension"
- e.g. "CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE", "Cardiovascular Disease", and "cardiovascular disease"
- e.g. "CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE", "Chronic Kidney Disease", and "chronic kidney disease"
- e.g. "TYPE 2 DIABETES", "Type 2 Diabetes", and "type 2 diabetes"

**Whitespace:** There were extra leading and trailing spaces around condition labels

- e.g. " Asthma "
- e.g. " Obesity "
- e.g. " Hypertension "
- e.g. " Cardiovascular Disease "
- e.g. " Chronic Kidney Disease "
- e.g. " Type 2 Diabetes "

**Underscores:** There were spaces replaced by underscores in column names

- e.g. "Chronic_Kidney_Disease", "Type_2_Diabetes", "Cardiovascular_Disease"

**5 missing value representations:** "" (empty strings), ".", "NA", "N/A", and "missing".

The dataset now has standard missing value notation and the comorbid_condition column has consistent syntax across all observations (N = 7200)

## 2b. Cleaning Numeric Fields

```{r}
# Retroactively add cols(.default = col_character())) to the CSV import step
# to have deliberate control of column type
```

Based on the unique values audited in Q2.a, several numeric variables contain commas, percent signs, currency symbols, units, and other extra characters.

We have documented the following issues across the dataset:

- **annual_household_income_usd:** "\$" and "," and "USD"
  - e.g. "\$60,829", "19732 USD"
- **area_deprivation_index_percentile:** "%" and " percent"
  - e.g. "42.5%", "39.8 percent"
- **sleep_duration_hours:** " h" and "hrs"
  - e.g. "8.2 h", "6.3hrs"
- **physical_activity_min_week"**: " min"
  - e.g. "161 min"
- **bmi_kg_m2:** "kg/m2" and "BMI"
  - e.g. "21.6 kg/m2", "30.2 BMI"
- **systolic_bp_mmHg:** "mm Hg" and "mmhg"
  - e.g. "134mm Hg", "106 mmHg"
- **total_cholesterol_mg_dL & fasting_glucose_mg_dL:** "mg/dl" and "mg_dl"
  - e.g. "165mg_dl", "67 mg/dl"
- **healthcare_visits_past_year:** "visits"
  - e.g. "5 visits"
- **phq9_score:** "score:" and "pts" and "points"
  - e.g. "score:11", "9 pts", "16 points"

```{r}
# Use across() and parse_number() to clean numeric fields discussed above
data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(
    c(annual_household_income_usd, area_deprivation_index_percentile, 
      sleep_duration_hours, physical_activity_min_week, bmi_kg_m2, 
      systolic_bp_mmHg, total_cholesterol_mg_dL, healthcare_visits_past_year, 
      phq9_score),
    parse_number
      )
  )      
```

## 2c. Removing Duplicates

There are 6 comorbid condition subsets in the dataset (Asthma, Cardiovascular Disease, Chronic Kidney Disease, Hypertension, Obesity, and Type 2 Diabetes.)

Each subset has a duplicate row, for a total of 6 duplicate rows that need to be removed, for an N = 7,194 (from 7,200).

```{r}
# Use distinct() to remove all duplicate rows
data <- data %>%
  distinct()
```

```{r}
# Identify rows where either prevalence or mortality values are missing
missing_vars <- data %>%
  # Use filter() to identify rows of NAs in each prevalence/mortality column
  filter(is.na(condition_prevalence_per_100k) | 
          is.na(condition_mortality_per_100k)) %>%
  # Select key columns (record_id), comorbid_condition) in addition to 
  # prevalence/mortality to create a df for easy scanning
  select(record_id, comorbid_condition, 
         condition_prevalence_per_100k, condition_mortality_per_100k) %>%
  as.data.frame()
# Print table of missing variables with key identifier columns
print(missing_vars)
```

Each comorbid condition has a missing prevalence and mortality value for a total of 12 records.

These missing prevalence and mortality values do not cause exclusion from the depression model because these variables are not called for in either the SLR or MLR models.

The MLR depression model, $\text{PHQ9}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{PhysicalActivity}_i) + \beta_2(\text{Age}_i) + \text{sex indicators} + \beta_{\text{income}}(\text{Income}_i) + \text{smoking indicators} + \varepsilon_i$, evaluates individual-level health relationships, opposed to contextual metrics like prevalence or mortality. Consequently, missing values in these variables will not affect any model parameters or analysis, so they do not warrant deletion from the depression model.

## 2d. Suspicious Value

```{r}
# Use summary() to identify the suspicious value in total_cholesterol_mg_dL
summary(data$total_cholesterol_mg_dL)
```

The variable total_cholesterol_mg_dL in this dataset primarily contains values from 85 mg/dL to about 300 mg/dL, but has one high outlier at 950 mg/dL. This value is far outside the norm in the dataset and in what is medically plausible. While it is not impossible for an individual to have an extreme reading like 950 mg/dL, it is more probable that this represents a data entry error, though this cannot be verified.

This suspicious value does not need to be removed from the dataset because it is not part of the primary MLR depression model, $\text{PHQ9}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{PhysicalActivity}_i) + \beta_2(\text{Age}_i) + \text{sex indicators} + \beta_{\text{income}}(\text{Income}_i) + \text{smoking indicators} + \varepsilon_i$. This outlier will neither affect calculations nor analysis, so it is safe to retain in the dataset.

## 2e. Complete-Case Analysis for Primary MLR

```{r}
# Perform a complete-case analysis for the primary MLR
analytic_data <- data %>%
  # Filter the dataset for our group's chosen condition subset
  filter(comorbid_condition == "cardiovascular disease") %>%
  # Restrict to complete cases on the 6 primary MLR variables only
  drop_na(
    phq9_score,
    physical_activity_min_week,
    age_years,
    sex,
    annual_household_income_usd,
    smoking_status
  )
# Export the cleaned analytic CSV for analysis into the data folder
write_csv(analytic_data, here::here("data", "cleaned_analytic_data.csv"))
```

The master CSV contained N = 7200 observations of 36 variables (1200 observations per comorbidity (6).

After standardizing the condition column and cleaning the numeric fields, we removed all duplicate rows (1 per comorbidity (6)), resulting in N = 7194.

After selecting cardiovascular disease as our comorbid condition, performing a complete-case analysis on the dataset results in a final N = 1075.

*Note: we opted to clean the entire master dataset prior to filtering (opposed to cleaning only our filtered dataset) to maintain a clean separation between the data cleaning phase and the analytic subsetting phase and to establish a clear and reproducible data management strategy.*
